Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Acute 3-day history of diarrhea with infra-umbilical crampy abdominal pain, urgency/tenesmus, borborygmi, nausea, and one episode of vomiting after eating fruit. No visible blood in stool or emesis. Uncertain fever (reported sweating), likely suboptimal fluid intake. Mild self-reported abdominal tenderness. Past history of asthma (uses inhaler). Family history significant for father with colorectal cancer.
- Most consistent with acute gastroenteritis. DDx supports: acute viral gastroenteritis (high likelihood) > acute bacterial gastroenteritis (medium). IBS-D considered less likely given acute onset.
- CRC considered unlikely for this acute presentation (DDx consistent), though family history noted; consider evaluation if symptoms persist or red flags develop.
- No red-flag features reported (no hematochezia, no severe persistent vomiting, no severe focal abdominal pain, no systemic toxicity) at time of call.

Management Plan
- Advise oral rehydration: increase fluids to prevent dehydration.
- Symptomatic care at home; rest and stay home until improving.
- Monitor for fever and worsening symptoms.
- Avoid antibiotics at this time; clinician advised they may worsen typical viral gastroenteritis.
- Safety-net: Seek in-person GP assessment if symptoms worsen, if unable to maintain hydration, if fever develops, if blood appears in stool or vomit, or if not improving within the next 1–2 days.
- Patient education: Likely infectious gastroenteritis; low likelihood of relation to family history of colorectal cancer for this acute episode; consider GP follow-up for further evaluation if persistent concerns.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Acute viral gastroenteritis – High likelihood: Acute onset of diarrhea with crampy abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, no blood or high fever; typical self-limited course.
- Acute bacterial gastroenteritis (foodborne) – Moderate likelihood: Similar presentation; lack of blood/high fever lowers likelihood.
- Irritable bowel syndrome, diarrhea-predominant (IBS-D) – Low likelihood: Pain relieved by defecation and urgency can fit but acute 3-day onset favors infection.
